bib.title: SEM: Reinforcement Learning for Search-Efficient Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "SEM: Reinforcement Learning for Search-Efficient Large Language Models", Zeyang Sha, Shiwen Cui, Weiqiang Wang (Ant Group). arXiv:2505.07903v1 [cs.CL], 12 May 2025. Venue: preprint ("Preprint. Under review."). First author Zeyang Sha.
COVERAGE: 12 of 12 pages read, 40502 of 40502 chars, including references. There is no appendix. Nothing skipped. No figure-caption script run; Figure 1 and 2 captions came from the text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. SEM trains the model to decide when to search, and it cuts search on questions that don't need it while keeping accuracy. Bears on note 07 (Search-R1-style RL, tool-call budgets) and note 05 (post-training for agents). The ReSearch baseline never learns the skip-search decision.
 number: MMLU 7B-Instruct search ratio (SR) 1.77% for SEM, vs 47.98% for Naive RAG. EM 70.88 vs ReSearch 69.84.
 setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 14B-Instruct. Trained on Musique+MMLU, 200 steps. Single run reported, no seeds or variance.
 quote: "MMLU 7B-Instruct Naive RAG 12.48 47.98% ReSearch 69.84 0.00% SEM 70.88 1.77%"
 where: Table 2, p6
2. On multi-hop QA, SEM keeps a high search rate (right for unknown questions) and raises EM over both baselines.
 number: HotpotQA 7B: SEM EM 35.84 / LJ 61.67 / SR 97.54%, vs Naive RAG 18.01 / 47.51 / 88.52% and ReSearch 21.75 / 32.06 / 0.08%. MuSiQue 7B: SEM 15.59 / 36.41 / 97.35% vs Naive RAG 7.19. HotpotQA 14B: SEM 40.42 EM vs Naive RAG 35.11, ReSearch 33.29. MuSiQue 14B: SEM 20.56 vs 13.52 and 14.43.
 setup: same as claim 1. EM is exact match, LJ is an LLM judge (deepseek-671B AWQ), SR is search ratio. Retrieval over wiki18-100w via FlashRAG.
 quote: "SEM 35.84 61.67 97.54%"
 where: Table 1, p5
 Caveat: at 14B the LJ score for SEM is below Naive RAG on HotpotQA (58.43 vs 59.55). The text still says SEM is "superior across all evaluated benchmarks", which Table 1 and Table 2 do not support.
3. Out-of-domain GSM8K shows a mixed picture. SEM avoids search, but accuracy is not uniformly better.
 number: 7B: SEM EM 71.79, SR 14.63%, vs ReSearch 82.63 at SR 0.00%. 14B: SEM 79.37, SR 0.76%, vs ReSearch 50.41 at SR 55.19% and Naive RAG 83.93 at SR 14.71%.
 setup: same as claim 1. The paper says the model is "only trained on MMLU" for this transfer, though training data is Musique+MMLU.
 quote: "SEM 79.37 0.76%" and "ReSearch 50.41 55.19%"
 where: Table 2, p6
 Caveat: the text says "Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct trained under SEM only invoke 0.76% search", but 0.76% is the 14B figure in Table 2. At 7B the table shows 14.63%.
4. SEM trains more smoothly than ReSearch.
 number: none (Figure 2 plots average F1 over 100 eval samples every checkpoint, 0 to 200 steps; y-axis tops out near 0.25).
 quote: "the ReSearch models suffer from larger fluctuations and slower gains in F1 score, particularly in the 7B setting."
 where: Sec 3.3, p6-7

REWARD DESIGN (p4, Eq. 1)
R = f · [ 1{F1(a1) ≥ τ ∧ s=0 ∧ t=1} · F1(a1) + 1{F1(a1) < τ ∧ u=1} · F1(a2) ]
- f is a valid-structure indicator. Bad format or tag order gives zero reward.
- a1 is the first <answer>, emitted before any search. If F1(a1) ≥ τ and no search was made (s=0) with a single think/answer (t=1), reward is F1(a1). Searching after a correct first answer therefore earns 0, which is the penalty.
- If F1(a1) < τ and the search-result format is valid (u=1), reward is F1(a2), the post-search answer.
- τ is the confidence threshold. Its value is not stated. Figure 2 says correct means F1 of 1.0.
- Template: think, answer (preliminary), search, result, think, answer (final).
- Optimizer is GRPO. Data is a balanced mix of Musique ("unknown" questions) and MMLU ("known" questions). The training mix ratio and the sizes are not given in numbers.
- This is not a per-call cost or a budget. It is a binary gate keyed on whether the first answer was right.
 quote: "If the first answer achieves a high F1 score (above a predefined threshold), but the model still invokes search or produces redundant reasoning steps, it is penalized for unnecessary exploration."
 where: p4

SETUP DETAILS (p5)
- Built on ReSearch [11], Verl [23] and FlashRAG [24]. Base models are Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 14B-Instruct.
- Hardware and training: 8 A100, batch size 8, 200 steps.
 quote: "we train the model for only 200 steps because, in the reinforcement learning setup, this number of updates is already sufficient to observe significant gains in performance."
 where: p5
- Eval sets: Musique, HotpotQA (search expected, so high SR is good) and MMLU, GSM8k (low SR is good).
- Baselines: Naive RAG and ReSearch, which the authors retrained on their own data. The paper says "our ReSearch results differ from the original paper due to discrepancies in training datasets."
- ReSearch's weak numbers are blamed on the dataset mix causing "gradient explosion". That is asserted, not shown.

ABLATIONS: none. There is no reward-term ablation, no threshold sweep, no data-mix ablation and no seeds. Search-R1 itself is not compared. The only baselines are Naive RAG and ReSearch.

LIMITS
- One run per cell and no variance. Only the Qwen2.5 family at 7B and 14B.
- No cost or latency numbers. "Efficiency" is measured only as search ratio.
- The reward assumes the model can emit a correct first answer without retrieval. The "known vs unknown" labelling is implicit in the data source, MMLU vs Musique. No calibration of actual model knowledge is shown.
- ReSearch at 7B ends with 0.08% SR on HotpotQA, so the baseline is effectively broken in their setup. This makes the comparison weak.
- The paper's own text contradicts its tables in places (claims 2 and 3). Table 2 gives Naive RAG 12.48 EM for both MMLU and GSM8K at 7B, which looks like a copy error.
- Case studies show only the 1+1 and Tyler Redenbach examples. Retrieved results are placeholders ("some result here").
- Authors do not state limitations explicitly.

BUILDS ON: ReSearch (Chen et al. [11], 2025), Verl (Sheng et al. [23]), FlashRAG (Jin et al. [24], 2024), GRPO (Shao et al. [16]), Musique [14], MMLU [15], HotpotQA [20], GSM8k [21], and [12] Feng et al. and [13] Zheng et al. (DeepResearcher). Search-R1 is not named in the extraction beyond the related-work citations [11–13].

CODE: none.

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p3) compares the old method, where the model "still wants to search due to my training law" on a known question, with SEM answering directly or searching only when unsure. Fig 2 (p7) plots average F1 against steps 0-200 for ReSearch and SEM at 7B and 14B. Tables 3 and 4 (p7-8) are the 1+1 and Tyler Redenbach traces.

SUGGESTED USE: it sharpens note 07 on tool-call budgets. It gives a first-answer-gated reward instead of a per-call penalty. The evidence is thin: a single run, two baselines, no ablations.

PROBLEMS: extraction was clean. No embedded instructions found. The text/table mismatches above are in the source itself.
